Я выбираю кандидата 7. Всё посчитано в уме на средних значениях спроса, поэтому цифры ниже приблизительные.

**Общий для всех убыток.** Товар 1 идёт 5 дней, поэтому в дни 0–4 продаётся только стартовый запас в 44 единицы. Спрос за эти дни около 158 единиц, и неустойку платят все кандидаты одинаково.

**Частота заказов.** Каждый день с заказом стоит 57, а средний переходящий запас дороже при длинном цикле.
- Ежедневные заказы (кандидат 2): около 27 дней × 57 ≈ 1540 фиксированных затрат. По сравнению с циклом в 2 дня это примерно на 740 больше, а экономия на хранении всего около 430. Кандидат 2 проигрывает.
- Цикл 2 дня против цикла 3 дня: на 4 дня с заказом больше, это +228. Зато средний запас меньше примерно на 22 единицы, и хранение обходится примерно на 430 дешевле. Цикл 2 дня выигрывает около 200.
- Цикл 4 дня (кандидаты 3 и 5): разовые приходы вроде 85 + 130 единиц плюс остатки не помещаются в склад на 188. Излишек пропадает, хотя уже оплачен. Это худший вариант.

**Объёмы.** Ожидаемый спрос с учётом среднего множителя 1,046: по товару 0 около 474, по товару 1 около 887.
- Кандидаты 0 и 6 закупают меньше всех, поэтому у них больше всего неустоек.
- Кандидаты 1 и 7 закупают почти одинаково: товар 1 около 812–813, товар 0 около 488–492. В среднем им всё ещё немного не хватает товара 1, но это лучший баланс. У кандидата 7 циклы по 2 дня, поэтому он дешевле кандидата 1 на хранении.
- Кандидат 4 закупает больше всех, но в 3-дневном цикле оба товара приходят в один день. Примерно в день 8 склад переполняется на ~21 единицу, в день 14 — на ~36, и теряется в основном товар 1. Ещё у него лишние ~57 единиц товара 0. В итоге запас товара 1 получается как у кандидата 1, а затраты на хранение и закупку выше.

**Устойчивость к случайности.** У кандидата 7 товар 0 приходит в чётные дни, а товар 1 в нечётные. Поэтому пиковая загрузка склада ниже, и при спросе ниже прогноза риск переполнения меньше, чем у планов с 3- и 4-дневными циклами.

Порядок по ожидаемому итогу: 7 > 1, 6 > 0, 4 > 2 > 3, 5.

**Choice: candidate 7.** I worked this out by hand on the forecast values and did not run a simulation. The order of 6 against 7 is less certain than the ranking by order frequency.

1. **How often to order.** Each order day costs 57, and stock costs about 0.65 per unit per day to hold. Total demand is about 45 units a day.
   - Ordering every 2 days (candidates 6 and 7): about 13 order days cost ≈ 740, plus holding ≈ 440. Total ≈ 1200.
   - Every 3 days (candidates 0, 1 and 4): about 570 plus ≈ 880. Total ≈ 1450.
   - Every 4 days (candidates 3 and 5): about 400 plus ≈ 1300. Total ≈ 1700. On top of that, peak stock comes close to the 188-unit limit.
   - Every day (candidate 2): 27 order days cost ≈ 1540 in fixed fees alone.
   - The standard order-size formula (EOQ) agrees: √(2·57·45/0.65) ≈ 89 units, which is about 2 days of demand.
2. **Shared losses.** Item 1 takes 5 days to arrive, so every plan runs short of it on days 2–4 (about 100 units). This doesn't separate the candidates.
3. **Capacity in the 3-day plans.** In candidates 0, 1 and 4, both items arrive on the same day. Candidate 4 then receives about 176–182 units plus leftovers, so some item 1 stock is lost to overflow.
4. **Safety stock under randomness.** A missing unit costs 6 in lost margin plus 6–7 in penalty. A surplus unit only costs holding, because it doesn't spoil within the 2-day cycle. So a margin above forecast pays off. Note that average demand is already about 4.6% above forecast.
   - Candidate 6 orders about 4–6% above forecast, which only covers that average.
   - Candidate 7 orders about 10–12% above forecast, leaving a real buffer.
   - Neither comes close to the warehouse limit.

That is why candidate 7 should have the highest expected profit.

**Choice: candidate 7.** I worked this out roughly in my head, as the task asked; I did not simulate every day exactly.

1. **Ordering every 4 days (candidates 3 and 5).** Each delivery is about 187–215 units, and stock left over from earlier goes on top of that. The warehouse holds 188, so part of each delivery is lost, and the holding cost is the highest of all the plans.
2. **Ordering every day (candidate 2).** That is about 28 orders × 57 ≈ 1,600 in fixed fees alone. That is too much.
3. **Every 3 days or every 2?** Both products together sell about 45 units a day.
   - The best order size is √(2·57·45/0.65) ≈ 89 units, which is about two days of demand.
   - Going from every 2 days to every 3 cuts the number of orders from 15 to 10. That saves about 5 × 57 = 285.
   - But the stock left each evening grows from about 22 to about 45 units. That adds about 22.5 × 0.65 × 30 ≈ 440 in holding cost.
   - So candidates 0, 1 and 4 (every 3 days) lose to candidates 6 and 7 (every 2 days). Every-2-days delivery sizes also stay well under the 188 limit.
4. **Candidate 6 or 7?** Both order every 2 days and differ only in order size.
   - Candidate 6 orders about two days of forecast demand. For example, it orders 35 of product 0 against 33 forecast and 70 of product 1 against 67.
   - Candidate 7 orders about 5–8 % more.
   - On average, actual demand runs about 4.6 % above the forecast.
   - Being short is expensive: about 12–13 per unit (lost margin plus the penalty). Having one unit too many costs only about 0.6–0.7 of holding per day, because the leftover is sold the next day.
   - So the extra margin pays off when demand comes in high, and candidate 7 holds up better than 6.

All plans hit the same unavoidable shortages at the start: product 0 on day 1, and product 1 on days 1–4, before the first delivery arrives on day 5. These don't separate the candidates.

I'd pick **candidate 7**. This is an estimate worked out in my head, not a simulation, so the margins between candidates are rough.

1. **How often to order.** Candidates 6 and 7 order every 2 days, which is 13 orders and 741 in fixed fees. That is the best trade-off between fixed fees and holding cost:
   - Combined demand is about 44 units a day, and holding averages about 0.65 per unit per day.
   - The standard order-size formula gives a cycle of about √(2·57 / (44·0.65)) ≈ 2 days.
   - Moving from 2-day to 3-day orders saves 228 in fees. But it adds about 22 units of average stock, which costs about 430 in holding over 30 days.
   - Moving from 3-day to 4-day orders has the same problem: it saves 114 and adds about 430.
   - Ordering every day (candidate 2) costs about 1425 in fees, which is clearly too much.
2. **Warehouse capacity.** In the 3-day plans, both goods arrive on the same mornings. In candidate 4, two of those arrivals (days 8 and 14) total 176–182 units before leftovers, so some of the incoming product 1 is likely lost. Candidates 3 and 5 (every 4 days) also come close to 188 when product 1 arrives. The 2-day plans don't have this risk.
3. **6 versus 7.** A missed unit of demand costs 12–13 (lost margin plus penalty). An extra unit in stock costs only about 0.65 a day, and with a 9-day shelf life it can still be sold later. So a small safety margin pays off:
   - Candidate 6 orders about the expected demand (for example 70 units of product 1 against about 70 expected for days 5–6).
   - Candidate 7 orders a bit more (74 in the same case).

**Choice: candidate 7.** I worked this out by rough mental estimates, not a full day-by-day simulation, so this is a well-supported best guess rather than a certainty.

**1. How often to order (fixed fee vs. holding cost)**

Total demand averages about 47 units a day.

| Cycle | Candidates | Fees (57 per order day) | Holding cost | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Daily | 2 | about 1600 | small | ≈ 1600 |
| Every 2 days | 6, 7 | 14 × 57 ≈ 800 | ≈ 15/day → ≈ 375 | ≈ 1175 |
| Every 3 days | 0, 1, 4 | 10 × 57 = 570 | ≈ 30/day → ≈ 750 | ≈ 1320 |
| Every 4 days | 3, 5 | 7 × 57 ≈ 400 | ≈ 45/day → ≈ 1125 | ≈ 1525 |

The 4-day plans also nearly fill the 188-unit warehouse: on arrival days stock reaches about 175 even at average demand. When demand runs low, the next delivery would overflow and paid-for units would be lost. The 2-day cycle comes out cheapest and is in no danger on capacity.

**2. How much to order (buffer above expected demand)**

The demand multiplier averages 1.046, so expected demand is above the forecast. Running out costs about 12–13 per unit (6 of lost margin plus a 6–7 penalty). Overstock mostly costs 0.6–0.7 per day of holding, because leftovers stay sellable for 9 days. A small buffer above expected demand therefore pays off.

| | Product 1 total ordered | Product 0 total ordered |
|---|---|---|
| Expected demand the deliveries must cover | ≈ 729 | ≈ 439 |
| Candidate 6 | 729 (no buffer) | 437 (no buffer) |
| Candidate 7 | 769 (about 5% above) | 465 (about 6% above) |
| Candidate 0 / 1 / 4 | 728 / 768 / 835 | — |

With a 30% daily spread in demand, candidate 6 would run short fairly often. Candidate 7's extra ~5% cuts shortages at a modest holding cost. Among the 3-day plans, candidate 4's larger quantities raise the risk of overflowing the warehouse on arrival days.

Candidate 7 combines the cheapest ordering cycle with a reasonable buffer.

I picked **candidate 7**. I estimated this in my head without running a simulation, so it's an estimate, not an exact calculation.

1. **How often to order.** Each order day costs 57 in fixed fees. Each unit held overnight costs about 0.65. Combined daily demand is about 45 units. The standard order-size formula gives √(2·57·45/0.65) ≈ 89 units, which is about 2 days of demand.
   - Ordering every 2 days (candidates 6 and 7) adds about 170 in fixed fees compared with every 3 days. It cuts holding costs by about 430, so it comes out about 260 ahead.
   - Ordering every 4 days (candidates 3 and 5) does worse still. Batches near 187 units also come close to the 188-unit warehouse limit, so some stock could be lost on arrival.
   - Ordering every day (candidate 2) pays the 57 fee about 28 times, roughly 1,600 in total, which is much worse.

2. **Candidate 6 vs 7.** Both order every 2 days, so the order sizes decide it.
   - From day 5 onward, the forecast demand for product 1 adds up to 697. Since demand averages about 4.6% above forecast, the expected real demand is about 729.
   - Candidate 6 orders exactly 729, so it carries no safety stock. Candidate 7 orders 769, about 5% more.
   - A shortage costs a lot: the lost 6-unit margin plus a 6–7 penalty. Extra stock costs only about 0.65 a day, and since shelf life is 9 days it carries over instead of being thrown away. So a little extra stock pays off, which favours candidate 7.

I pick **candidate 7**: it orders every 2 days with slightly larger quantities, and that gives the best expected profit. I worked this out by hand-tracing the rules on the forecast (mean) values; nothing was simulated.

**1. What every plan shares.** Item 1 takes 5 days to arrive, so on days 1–4 every plan runs out of item 1. That costs about 107 units × 6 ≈ 640 in penalties for all of them. The plans really differ in four ways: how often they order (57 per order day), how much stock they hold, whether they run short of cash, and how much spare stock they carry against random demand.

**2. Ordering cost vs. holding cost.** Demand is about 45 units a day and holding costs about 0.65 per unit per day. In a cycle of k days the extra stock left overnight averages about (k−1)/2 days of demand. Over roughly 25 days that gives:

| Order interval | Candidates | Order fees | Holding (approx.) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Daily | 2 | 28 × 57 = 1596 | ≈ 0 | ≈ 1596 |
| Every 2 days | 6, 7 | 14 × 57 = 798 | ≈ 375 | ≈ 1170 |
| Every 3 days | 0, 1, 4 | 10 × 57 = 570 | ≈ 750 | ≈ 1320 |
| Every 4 days | 3, 5 | 7 × 57 = 399 | ≈ 1125 | ≈ 1525 |

The 2-day cycle is cheapest.

**3. Cash and warehouse space.**
- **Every 4 days (3, 5):** cash runs short on day 4, so the item 1 order is cut. Candidate 3 gets 102 units instead of 130, and candidate 5 gets 107 instead of 129. That leaves item 1 short on days 9–12. These plans also come close to the 188-unit warehouse limit when a large item 1 delivery arrives.
- **Every 3 days:** candidate 1 is cut on day 6 (item 1 gets about 83 units instead of 100). Candidate 4, which orders even more, would be cut harder. Candidate 0 just barely has the cash.
- **Every 2 days (6, 7):** orders are small, so there's always enough cash. Candidate 7 has about 983 left after its day-2 order.

**4. Random demand, candidate 6 vs. 7.** Running short costs a lot: about 13 per unit (the lost margin of 6 plus a penalty of 6–7). A leftover unit costs little, because it keeps for 9 days and is sold in the next cycle for about 1.2 extra holding. So ordering above forecast pays off, especially since the average demand multiplier is 1.046. Candidate 6 orders roughly forecast × 1.05; candidate 7 orders about 6% more. Candidate 7 is closer to the right level and holds up better when demand is high.

I picked **candidate 7**. I worked this out by hand-estimating the plans, not by simulating them, so it's a judgement call rather than a calculation.

1. **How often to order.** Each order day has a fixed fee of 57, and stock left in the warehouse costs about 0.65 per unit per day.
   - **Every day (candidate 2):** about 1,425 in fixed fees alone, far too much.
   - **Every 4 days (candidates 3 and 5):** each delivery is about 185–190 units. Add whatever is left over and it goes past the 188-unit limit, so units overflow and are lost after being paid for.
   - **Every 2 days vs every 3 days:** ordering every 2 days costs about 285 more in fixed fees. It cuts the average evening stock by about 22 units, which saves about 440 in storage. So every 2 days comes out ahead by about 150.

2. **How much to order.** I compared each plan's total order with the expected demand it can actually serve. Demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, and I left out the early days before the first order can arrive.
   - **Candidates 0 and 6:** about 729 units of product 1 and about 437 of product 0. That matches the expected demand almost exactly, with no safety margin.
   - **Candidates 1 and 7:** about 5% more (+40 of product 1, +26 of product 0).
   - **Candidate 4:** about another 5% on top of that.

3. **Which way the risk leans.** Running short costs about 12–13 per unit (the penalty plus the lost 6 margin). An extra unit only costs a few days of storage, because it carries over and sells later. Demand is random and the plan is fixed in advance, so a moderate surplus pays off. That points to the 2-day plan with the 5% margin.

I estimated this by reasoning, not by simulating it, so it's a judgement call rather than an exact calculation.

**I pick candidate 7.**

1. **How often to order.** Each order day costs a flat 57. Ordering less often means fewer fees but more stock sitting on the shelf each night, and that costs storage. Daily demand for both items together is about 45 units, and storage averages about 0.65 per unit per day.
   - **Every 3 days vs every 4 days (candidates 3 and 5):** ordering every 4 days skips about 3 orders, saving roughly 170. It also leaves about 22 more units on hand each evening, costing roughly 400 extra over the month. Those plans also run close to the 188-unit limit, so some stock could be lost when deliveries arrive.
   - **Every 2 days vs every 3 days (candidates 6 and 7):** ordering every 2 days adds 4 orders, about 230. It saves roughly 400 in storage, so the 2-day cycle comes out ahead.
   - **Every day (candidate 2):** this adds about 14 more orders (around 800) to save another ~400 in storage, so it loses.
2. **How much to order.** Candidates 6 and 7 both order every 2 days. A missed sale costs about 13 (6 lost profit plus a 6–7 penalty). An extra unit costs only about 0.65 a day to store, and unsold stock carries over to later days. Actual demand also averages about 4.6% above the forecast. So a bit of extra stock pays off. Candidate 6 orders roughly the expected demand; candidate 7 orders about 7% more. With orders this size, the 188-unit limit isn't a problem for either.

**Choice: Candidate 7.** I worked this out by hand on the forecast averages, with rough estimates rather than an exact day-by-day simulation.

1. **Ordering every 2 days (candidates 6 and 7) costs the least overall.** Each order day costs 57, and stock sitting in the warehouse costs 0.6–0.7 per unit per day. Demand is about 45 units a day for both products together.
   - **Daily ordering (candidate 2):** about 28 order days × 57 ≈ 1600 in order fees. Storage is small, about 450. Total ≈ 2050.
   - **Every 2 days (6, 7):** about 15 × 57 ≈ 855 in fees. Each delivery is half used up on average, so about 45 units sit in stock, costing ≈ 880. Total ≈ 1735.
   - **Every 3 days (0, 1, 4):** about 10 × 57 = 570 in fees, but about 67 units sit in stock, costing ≈ 1300. Total ≈ 1870.
   - **Every 4 days (3, 5):** about 400 in fees, but about 90 units sit in stock, costing ≈ 1750. Total ≈ 2150. These two also overflow the warehouse: one order of 85 + 130 = 215 is more than the 188-unit capacity, so units are lost.

2. **The 3-day plans risk losing units to overflow.** With a 3-day cycle, product 0 (2-day delivery) and product 1 (5-day delivery) arrive on the same days. Candidate 4 on day 8 receives 78 + 104 = 182 units plus leftovers, which overflows. Candidate 1 receives 165 plus leftovers, which is close to the limit. In the 2-day plans, product 0 arrives on even days and product 1 on odd days, so there is no overflow.

3. **Between 6 and 7, the larger orders win.** A missing unit costs 13 for product 0 (6 lost margin + 7 penalty) and 12 for product 1. A spare unit costs only 0.6–0.7 a day to store, and with a 9-day shelf life almost nothing gets written off. Actual demand averages about 4.6% above the forecast, so the extra stock in candidate 7 pays for itself. It also holds up better when demand jumps.

Every plan runs short of product 1 on days 1–4, because the first delivery can't arrive before day 5, so that loss doesn't separate the candidates.

I picked candidate 1. I worked this out by hand with rough numbers, not a full day-by-day simulation, and candidates 1 and 4 come out close.

**How the plans compare**

- **Candidates 3 and 5 (order every 4 days)** are the worst. A single delivery reaches 85 + 130 = 215 units, which is more than the 188-unit warehouse holds. The extra spoils on arrival, and those units were already paid for.
- **Candidate 2 (order every day)** pays the 57 fee about 28 times, roughly 1,600 in total. Every other plan pays it only 10 to 15 times.
- **Candidates 6 and 7 (order every 2 days)** keep too little spare stock. Each order barely covers the forecast for its two days. With a shortfall costing about 12–13 per unit and holding about 2 per unit, the extra shortages and penalties cost more than these plans save on storage.
- **Candidates 0, 1 and 4 (order every 3 days)** are the most balanced. Here the size of the spare stock decides it:
  - Candidate 0's orders roughly equal average demand, so it runs short fairly often.
  - Candidate 4 has nearly the ideal spare stock on paper, about one standard deviation of demand. But its deliveries plus leftovers come close to 188 and go over it: on day 8 it is about 182 + 23 ≈ 205, and on day 14 about 176 + 23 ≈ 199. My rough estimate is that overflow wastes about 240 in purchases over the month. That is more than the roughly 150 it gains from fewer shortages compared with candidate 1.
  - Candidate 1 has slightly less spare stock, but its deliveries stay under the limit at about 165–177 units. It loses only a little to shortages and almost nothing to overflow.

Because the two estimates are so close, candidate 4 could come out ahead if demand is often higher than forecast. On expected value, candidate 1 is the best of the eight.

I picked **candidate 7**: it reorders every 2 days and keeps a moderate safety margin. I worked this out by hand, as the rules require, using approximate figures, so the conclusion is likely rather than certain.

**1. Order frequency.** Each day with an order costs 57. Holding costs about 0.65 per unit per day. Combined demand is about 43 units per day. For a cycle of T days, the rough daily cost is 57/T for orders plus about 14·(T−1) for holding, since stock is counted in the evening after sales:
- Daily ordering (candidate 2): about 57 per day, and 30 orders cost 1710 in fees. This is the worst option.
- Every 2 days (candidates 6, 7): about 42.5 per day. This is the cheapest.
- Every 3 days (candidates 0, 1, 4): about 47 per day.
- Every 4 days (candidates 3, 5): about 61 per day. These also risk going over the 188-unit warehouse limit (for example, 85 + 130 on day 4), and any excess is lost on arrival.

**2. Safety margin.** A shortage costs about 12–13 per unit: the lost margin of 6 plus the penalty of 6–7. Holding one extra unit costs only 0.6–0.7 per day. Leftover stock carries over, and the 9-day shelf life is rarely reached, so it pays to order somewhat above the forecast. Average demand is also about 1.046 × forecast, not 1.0.
- Candidate 6 orders about 1.06 × forecast, which is barely above average demand. Early in the month it will often run short.
- Candidate 7 orders about 1.12 × forecast. The extra stock builds up gradually and absorbs random swings in demand.
- Candidate 4 orders about 1.2 × forecast, which is too much. Roughly 190 surplus units would be paid for and never sold, about 950 lost, plus the holding cost.
- Among the 3-day plans, candidate 0 is too lean (about 1.02 × forecast). Candidate 1 has a margin similar to candidate 7 but pays more in combined order and holding costs.

Candidate 7 has the cheapest order schedule and a sound buffer against shortages, with no capacity risk.

I picked **candidate 7**. I estimated this in my head without simulating, so it's an estimate, not an exact calculation.

1. **Order frequency matters most.** Each order day costs a fixed 57. Average daily demand is about 15 + 29 = 44 units, and holding costs about 0.65 per unit per day. If you order every T days, the cost per day is roughly 57/T plus 0.65 × 44 × T / 2, which is about 57/T + 14.3·T:
   - T = 1 (candidate 2): about 57 per day. Plus, because it orders exactly the forecast, it often runs short when demand comes in high.
   - T = 2 (candidates 6 and 7): about 57 per day. This is the cheapest option.
   - T = 3 (candidates 0, 1, 4): about 62 per day.
   - T = 4 (candidates 3, 5): about 71 per day. These orders are also close to the 188 warehouse limit, so some units may be lost on arrival.
2. **Choosing between 6 and 7.** Both order every 2 days. A missing unit costs 7 or 6 in penalty plus the lost margin of 6, so about 12–13. An extra unit costs only about 0.6–0.7 a day to store and doesn't spoil, because shelf life is 9 days. Real demand runs about 4.6% above the forecast on average. So it pays to order a bit high. Candidate 7 orders slightly more than candidate 6 (for example, 37 vs 35 units of product 0 on day 0), which should mean fewer shortages for very little extra storage.

I'd pick **candidate 7**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation.

1. **How often to order.** Total demand is about 45 units a day. Ordering every k days, the average end-of-day stock is roughly 45·(k−1)/2, and storage costs about 0.65 per unit per day.
   - Every 2 days instead of every 3 saves about 22 units of stock a day. That is about 440 in storage over 30 days. It costs 3 extra orders, which is 171. So every 2 days is better.
   - Every day instead of every 2 saves about 440 more in storage. But it needs 12 more orders, which is about 684. So daily ordering is worse.
   - Every 4 days saves on orders but costs more in storage. Those plans also bring stock close to the 188-unit limit, so a high-demand stretch could cause overflow losses.

   That makes every 2 days the best schedule. Candidates 6 and 7 use it.
2. **How much to order.** A missing unit costs 13: the 7 penalty plus the 6 margin lost. A unit left over costs only about 0.65 a day in storage and carries over to the next days. Spoilage is unlikely because goods keep for 9 days. So it's worth ordering a little above expected demand.
   - Candidate 6 orders about the average 2-day demand. Since the plan is fixed and unmet demand is simply lost, stock would often run out.
   - Candidate 7 orders about 6% more, which builds a small buffer against shortages.

I picked **candidate 1**. I worked the numbers roughly in my head, so the gap between candidates 1 and 4 is small and not certain.

1. **Daily ordering (candidate 2) loses the most.** The 57 fee is paid on 28 order days, about 1,600 in total. The lower storage cost doesn't come close to making that back.

2. **Ordering every 4 days (candidates 3 and 5) overflows the warehouse.** On some days the deliveries alone go past 188. For example, candidate 3's day-4 order is 85 + 130 = 215 units, and both items arrive together. The extra units are lost after being paid for. Storage costs are also higher, because about 1.5 days of demand sits in stock on average.

3. **Every 2 days (candidates 6 and 7) versus every 3 days (candidates 0, 1 and 4):**
   - The 2-day plans pay the 57 fee 5 more times (about 285), but save about 400 in storage.
   - However, their margin over expected demand is thin: about 4–6% for candidate 6 and about 10% for candidate 7. Actual demand averages about 4.6% above forecast, so this barely covers the mean.
   - A shortage unit costs about 12 (6 lost margin plus a penalty of 6–7), while holding a unit for 3 days costs about 2. So the larger buffers of the 3-day plans pay off: they cut expected shortages by several hundred.

4. **Choosing among the 3-day plans:**
   - Candidate 0 orders close to plain forecast demand, so it runs short often.
   - Candidate 4 has a buffer of about 20%, but it hits the capacity limit. On day 8, 78 + 104 = 182 units arrive on top of leftover stock, and on day 14 it is 54 + 122 = 176. Units overflow and are lost after being paid for, and storage costs on the extra stock add up.
   - Candidate 1, with a buffer of about 14%, sits between them. It runs short noticeably less often than candidate 0 and mostly stays under the 188 limit (on day 8 it is about 165 plus leftovers).

**Unavoidable at the start:** item 1 will run short on days 1–4 in every plan, because the first order can't arrive before day 5.

Я выбираю **кандидата 1**, уверенность средняя. Всё посчитано в уме на прогнозных значениях с поправкой на средний множитель 1,046.

- **Кандидат 2 (заказ каждый день):** около 27 платежей по 57, это примерно 1540 одних фиксированных затрат. Планы с циклом в 3 дня платят только 9 раз, около 510. Ежедневный заказ почти ничего не даёт взамен, поэтому этот план хуже всех.
- **Кандидаты 6 и 7 (заказ раз в 2 дня):** 13 заказов вместо 9, то есть лишние ~230 фиксированных затрат. Цикл в 3 дня и так укладывается во вместимость склада, так что эти деньги не окупаются.
- **Кандидаты 3 и 5 (заказ раз в 4 дня):** поставки приходят крупными партиями. Товар 0 приходит через 2 дня после заказа, товар 1 — через 5, поэтому обе партии приходят в одни и те же дни. The classic best order size is √(2·57·45/0.65) ≈ 89 units, which is about two days of demand. So ordering every 2 days should beat the other cycles:
- **Daily orders (candidate 2):** 28 order days cost about 1600, which outweighs everything else.
- **Every 3 days (0, 1, 4):** 10 order days instead of 13 saves about 171. But average stock is about 22 units higher, which costs about 22 · 0.65 · 30 ≈ 430 in storage. The 3-day plans also need more safety stock.
- **Every 4 days (3, 5):** storage costs even more, and the warehouse cap of 188 is close. For example, candidate 3 orders 125 of product 1 on day 0, and demand on the days that delivery covers (days 5–8) is about 117. That leaves almost no safety margin.
- **Every 2 days (6, 7):** closest to the best cycle length.

**2. Safety stock.** A shortage costs 6 lost margin plus a 6–7 penalty, so about 12 per unit. A surplus unit only costs storage (about 0.65 per day) and carries over to the next days. So it pays to order noticeably above the average forecast. The demand multiplier also averages 1.046, so actual demand runs slightly above forecast.
- Candidate 6 orders almost exactly the forecast. For example, 70 units of product 1 on day 0 against demand of 67 on days 5–6.
- Candidate 7 orders 74 in the same spot, which is higher and therefore more resilient when demand runs high. For two days of demand the spread is about 14 units, so even 7 has less buffer than the ideal.

**3. Product 1 shortage at the start.** Product 1 takes 5 days to arrive. The starting 44 units can't cover days 0–4 (demand about 151), so every plan takes the same early penalty. It doesn't change the ranking.

Candidate 7 has the right cycle length and the larger safety margin, so it should have the highest expected profit.

I picked **candidate 1**. It's a mental estimate, not an exact simulation.

1. **Every-4-day plans (candidates 3 and 5) lose to the warehouse limit.** On arrival days, the order alone is about 215 units (for example 85 + 130). That is more than the 188-unit capacity, so some of it is lost after being paid for. Their storage cost is also the highest.

2. **Daily ordering (candidate 2) pays too much in fees.** Ordering 28 days at 57 each costs about 1600 in fees. A 3-day cycle costs about 19 per day in fees plus about 28 per day in extra storage. That is much cheaper than 57 per day.

3. **The every-2-day plans (6 and 7) and the every-3-day plans (0, 1 and 4) are close on costs.** Plans 6 and 7 keep very little spare stock, especially of product 1. A unit short costs about 12–13 (6 lost margin plus a 6–7 penalty). A spare unit costs only about 2 in storage over a cycle and does not spoil, since it can be sold for 9 days. So the right amount of spare stock is fairly high, and 6 and 7 are below it.

4. **Among the 3-day plans, the choice is 0, 1 or 4.**
   - **Candidate 0** keeps the least spare stock, so it will run short more often.
   - **Candidate 4** keeps the most spare stock but hits the 188 limit. Both products arrive on the same days. On day 8 it receives 78 + 104 = 182 units plus about 20 left over, which spills about 15 units of product 1. On day 14 it is about 54 + 122 + 25 ≈ 200, spilling about 13. The extra spare stock gains roughly 140. The spill and the shortages it causes cost about the same or more, and this gets worse when demand varies.
   - **Candidate 1** keeps enough spare stock (somewhat less than the ideal) and its peak is about 177–182, still under 188. That makes it the most stable when demand differs from the forecast.
